Katukina is a name used for two different peoples of western Brazil. One group speaks a Katukinan language, close to Kanamari, in the state of Amazonas. The other, in Acre, speaks a Panoan language and calls itself Noke Koî. The shape on this map, near the upper Juruá River in Acre, matches the Panoan group.

The Panoan Katukina are kin to the Yawanawá, the Marubo and the Shawanaua, and neighbours of the Huni Kuin. During the rubber boom of the late 1800s, tappers moved into the Juruá valley and many Native people were forced to work for them. Today the Katukina hold land along the BR-364 highway in Brazil.
